cards.front: Yeast-induced pyrexia: what is it?
cards.back: A rat fever model. A subcutaneous dried-yeast suspension raises body temperature after about 18 h. Only rats with a rise of at least 0.6 °C are used to test an antipyretic against a standard such as aspirin.
refs: WEB PMC Screening of anti-inflammatory and antipyretic activity of Vitex leucoxylon Linn 2010 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2991704/

cards.front: Short note: Experimental methods to evaluate antipyretic activity

points: Antipyretics lower fever, so the model first raises body temperature and then measures the fall
Yeast-induced pyrexia in rats is the standard screen
Inject a 20% dried-yeast suspension in 2% gum acacia, subcutaneously, about 20 mL/kg
After about 18 h, select rats whose temperature rose by at least 0.6 °C
Give the test drug orally; aspirin is the standard (reference) drug
Groups: febrile control (vehicle), standard (aspirin), test drug at graded doses
Record temperature at fixed intervals and compare the fall with the control
Check that the drug does not lower the temperature of normal, non-febrile animals (a true antipyretic does not)
Some rats show hypothermia rather than fever, so animals must be screened first
Rodent fever is not identical to human fever; confirm hits in a second model
Done after acute and repeated-dose tests, before human trials
Special tests: reproduction and teratogenicity (pregnant animals, organogenesis), mutagenicity (Ames test, in-vitro cell tests), carcinogenicity (long-term dosing, rodents)
Regulatory: studies follow GLP; repeated-dose tests use a rodent and a non-rodent species; duration matches the planned clinical use; CDSCO (Schedule Y, NDCT Rules) sets the framework

refs: WEB PMC Screening of anti-inflammatory and antipyretic activity of Vitex leucoxylon Linn 2010 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2991704/

cards.front: Neurotoxicity screening of a new drug: what is it?
cards.back: Preclinical check in rodents for CNS effects (behaviour, motor, autonomic, sensory) before human trials. Regulators expect it under ICH S7A.
refs: WEB PMC Single-Dose Oral Administration of Theophylline in ICR Mice: Modified Irwin Test 2026 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12973419/

cards.front: Short note: Screening the neurotoxic potential of a new drug

points: CNS safety is part of safety pharmacology
Regulators (ICH S7A) expect a neurobehavioural screen before human trials
Modified Irwin test or functional observational battery (FOB)
Rodents, usually mice or rats, dosed and observed
Score about 18 endpoints with a semi-quantitative system
Observe at baseline (0 h) and at fixed times after dosing, e.g. 1, 2, 4, 6 and 24 h
Survival and general condition
Neuromuscular and motor: locomotion, tremor, convulsion
Autonomic: body temperature, eyelid closure
Reflexes and sensory responses
Rotarod for motor coordination
Open-field test for locomotor and exploratory activity
Scoring is subjective and prone to observer bias
No neurotransmitter, receptor or electrophysiology data, so add objective measures

refs: WEB PMC Single-Dose Oral Administration of Theophylline in ICR Mice: Modified Irwin Test 2026 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12973419/

cards.front: Earthworm acute toxicity test: what is it used for?
cards.back: A rapid bioassay that measures acute toxicity of a substance directly in soil, using earthworms (Eisenia foetida) as test organisms. It is a modification of OECD 207 and can detect toxicity from contaminants bound to soil particles that filter-paper tests may miss.
refs: WEB PMC Soil contact bioassay for rapid determination of acute toxicity with Eisenia foetida 2019 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6940645

cards.front: Short note: Earthworm acute lethality test

points: Measures acute toxicity of a test substance to earthworms, used as an ecotoxicity screen for soil
Modification of OECD Test 207 (earthworm acute toxicity)
Test organism: Eisenia foetida
Soil contact bioassay: thin layer of moistened soil with the test substance in the test jar, worms added
Observation at 24 h and 48 h
Main endpoint: mortality, reported as percentage
Also recorded: biomass change, response to stimulus, sublethal signs (inflamed clitellus, expulsion of coelomic or bloody fluid)
Control mortality should be 10% or less (OECD acceptance threshold cited by the source)
Rapid and cheap, but standard acute assays give limited information on hazard to soil organisms overall

refs: WEB PMC Soil contact bioassay for rapid determination of acute toxicity with Eisenia foetida 2019 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6940645

cards.front: Charcoal meal test: what does it measure?
cards.back: In vivo propulsive motility in mice: how far an orally given charcoal marker travels through the small intestine, expressed as a percentage of total small-intestine length.
refs: WEB PMC PMC7168896 Biopolymer Extracted from Anadenanthera colubrina (Red Angico Gum): Antidiarrheal Activity and Safety, mice charcoal meal https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7168896/

cards.front: Short note: Assay of a drug affecting intestinal motility

points: Measures transit of a non-absorbed marker along the gut
Slowing of transit suggests antimotility or antidiarrhoeal action; speeding suggests purgative action
Fast animals briefly, then give test drug or vehicle orally or s.c.
After the set interval, give activated charcoal suspension orally
Sacrifice after a fixed time, lay out the small intestine and measure the charcoal front
Transit (%) = distance travelled by charcoal front / total small-intestine length x 100
Compare with vehicle (maximal propulsion) and a reference drug
Vehicle group as negative control
Atropine as a reference that reduces transit
Loperamide as a reference antimotility agent
Whole-animal assay: absorption and central effects can change transit
Isolated gut preparations separate direct smooth-muscle action

refs: WEB PMC PMC7168896 Biopolymer Extracted from Anadenanthera colubrina (Red Angico Gum): Antidiarrheal Activity and Safety, mice charcoal meal https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7168896/

cards.front: Ovalbumin-sensitised animal model (anti-asthmatic screen)
cards.back: Animal is sensitised to the antigen ovalbumin, then challenged with it to produce bronchospasm and airway inflammation; used to test whether a drug blocks the allergic airway response.

cards.front: Short note: In vivo models for antiasthmatic activity

points: Mimic allergic asthma: sensitisation then antigen challenge
Test drug blocks bronchospasm or airway hyperresponsiveness
Ovalbumin-sensitised, challenged by aerosol or intravenously
Histamine, acetylcholine or methacholine-induced bronchospasm
Anaesthetised ventilated (Konzett-Rössler type) preparation: rise in intratracheal pressure
Time to convulsions or collapse
Percent inhibition of bronchospasm versus vehicle
Dose-response, compared with standard drugs
Sensitisation and challenge protocols vary between labs
Model may not match human late-phase response
Standard drugs (salbutamol, theophylline, steroids) used as positive controls

cards.front: Experimental glaucoma: how is raised IOP produced in animal models?
cards.back: By blocking aqueous outflow (trabecular meshwork or episcleral/collector veins), or by abruptly narrowing the angle, so pressure rises and optic nerve and retinal ganglion cell damage can be studied.
refs: WEB PMC Evangelho, Mastronardi, de-la-Torre - Experimental Models of Glaucoma: A Review of the Literature 2019 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6630440

cards.front: Short note: Experimental models of acute congestive and chronic simple glaucoma

points: Principle: abrupt IOP rise that mimics an angle-closure attack
Reperfusion ischaemia model: anterior chamber paracentesis with a saline reservoir raises IOP very high and blocks retinal and uveal blood flow; pressure is then released
Laser photocoagulation plus temporary angle narrowing by paracentesis: abrupt rise lasting weeks, with marked retinal ganglion cell loss
Limits: inflammation, ischaemia and corneal opacity; ganglion cell loss is not seen in human POAG
Angle-closure-like genetic and canine models: beagle dogs develop angle closure and cupping over months to years; PRSS56-mutant mice have short axial length and a narrow angle
Principle: slow, progressive rise in IOP by reducing outflow
Hypertonic saline into episcleral veins (rat): moderate IOP rise over about 7-10 days with high variability; progressive ganglion cell loss; used for neuroprotection studies
Laser photocoagulation of the trabecular meshwork: repeated applications to raise IOP; synechiae, hyphaema and corneal oedema are drawbacks
Microbead (latex microsphere) injection: blocks trabecular outflow; repeated injections sustain the rise
Episcleral vein cauterisation and nylon suture vein occlusion: moderate, sustained pressure rise
Intracameral hyaluronic acid (rat, rabbit): raises IOP for days, leaves outflow largely open
Steroid-induced ocular hypertension (rabbit) and genetic models (DBA/2J mice): progressive rise, often months to develop

refs: WEB PMC Evangelho, Mastronardi, de-la-Torre - Experimental Models of Glaucoma: A Review of the Literature 2019 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6630440

cards.front: Short note: Preclinical evaluation of a new diuretic

points: Single-dose in vivo screen: urine volume and urinary electrolytes after the test drug are compared with a control and with a diuretic standard run in parallel.
Furosemide is the standard because it is the prototype high-ceiling diuretic (KDT8 ch42); loop diuretics can excrete up to 25% of the filtered Na+ load, against about 5% for thiazides (GG14 ch29).
Healthy adult male Wistar rats of 180-200 g.
Food and water are withdrawn 5 hours before dosing.
Each rat is kept alone in a metabolic cage, so that all the urine passed can be collected and measured.
Groups: a control group, furosemide 5 mg/kg, and three doses of the test compound (12.5, 25 and 50 mg/kg in the cited study).
All doses are given orally as a suspension in 0.5% w/v carboxymethyl cellulose.
A saline load of 5 ml/100 g of 0.9% NaCl by gavage provides enough urine flow for measurement.
Urine is collected for 0-5 hours and then for 5-24 hours, and volume and pH are read immediately.
Sodium and potassium are estimated by flame photometry and chloride by argentometric titration.
Diuretic index and diuretic activity are then calculated against the control and the standard.
A diuretic index above 1 means more urine than the control; a diuretic activity below 1 means weaker than furosemide (cleistanthin A and B in the cited study).
The timing separates a slow compound, active only in the 5-24 hour sample, from a fast one like furosemide.
The electrolyte pattern shows whether the natriuresis is accompanied by loss of potassium.
The response was not dose dependent in the cited study, so it is the three-dose design that shows this; a single dose would not have.
Urine output per hour was too small to measure, so only the 0-5 h and 5-24 h blocks are compared and the onset of action cannot be timed.
No attempt was made to explain the mechanism of the diuresis.

refs: WEB PMC Parasuraman & Raveendran, Diuretic effects of cleistanthin A and cleistanthin B in Wistar rats, J Young Pharm 2012 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3385220/

cards.front: What is the Lipschitz test?
cards.back: The standard rat screen for diuretic activity: after a short fast the rat is kept in a metabolic cage, the drug is given orally with a saline load, and urine volume plus sodium, potassium and chloride excretion are compared with a control and with furosemide.
refs: WEB PMC Parasuraman & Raveendran, Diuretic effects of cleistanthin A and cleistanthin B in Wistar rats, J Young Pharm 2012 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3385220/

cards.front: What is a metabolic cage used for in a diuretic experiment?
cards.back: It houses one rat at a time, so all the urine passed in a set period after dosing (0-5 h, then 5-24 h) can be collected and measured.
refs: WEB PMC Parasuraman & Raveendran, Diuretic effects of cleistanthin A and cleistanthin B in Wistar rats, J Young Pharm 2012 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3385220/

cards.front: Short note: Evaluation of a new antimalarial agent (in vitro and in vivo)

points: P. falciparum is grown by the Trager-Jensen method in RPMI 1640 with a serum substitute, hypoxanthine, HEPES and gentamicin; a chloroquine-resistant K1 strain was used in the cited study.
Thin Giemsa-stained smears under oil immersion give the parasitaemia, and 5% sorbitol selects synchronised ring-stage parasites.
The compound is serially diluted (about 1.6-100 micrograms/ml) against synchronised parasites.
Viability is read with the parasite lactate dehydrogenase (pLDH) assay, and the IC50 comes from the dose-response curve.
The same compound is tested on a mammalian cell line by MTT to obtain a cytotoxic CC50 (Vero cells in the cited study).
Selectivity index = CC50 divided by antiparasitic IC50; the active extract in the example had an index of about 23.
Rodent malaria parasite: P. berghei ANKA in mice; donor blood is collected at 20-30% parasitaemia and diluted in saline.
Each mouse receives 1 x 10^7 parasitised erythrocytes in 0.2 ml intraperitoneally.

sections.h: In vivo: Peters' four-day suppressive test
points: The drug is given orally at 3, 24, 48 and 72 hours after infection, with a vehicle group and chloroquine 25 mg/kg as controls.
A Giemsa smear on day 4 gives the parasitaemia, and percentage suppression = (control minus treated) / control x 100.
Suppression rises with dose in an active compound (42%, 71% and 77% at 200, 400 and 600 mg/kg in the cited study), and more than 50% suppression is read as moderate activity.
Separate acute oral toxicity study by OECD 425: one oral dose of 2000 mg/kg in mice, watched for 14 days.
Liver (ALT, AST, ALP) and kidney (BUN, creatinine) markers, plus liver and kidney histology, are checked for damage.

refs: WEB PMC Phuwajaroanpong et al., In vitro and in vivo antiplasmodial activities and acute oral toxicity of Blumea balsamifera leaf extracts, Plants 2026 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13708541/

cards.front: What is Peters' four-day suppressive test?
cards.back: A rodent antimalarial screen: mice infected with P. berghei are dosed orally on four successive days from 3 hours after infection, and the day-4 Giemsa smear gives the percentage suppression of parasitaemia against untreated controls.
refs: WEB PMC Phuwajaroanpong et al., In vitro and in vivo antiplasmodial activities and acute oral toxicity of Blumea balsamifera leaf extracts, Plants 2026 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13708541/

cards.front: What does the pLDH assay measure in antimalarial screening?
cards.back: Parasite lactate dehydrogenase, an enzyme of living P. falciparum; the signal falls as parasites are killed, so it is used to read viability in vitro and to calculate an IC50.
refs: WEB PMC Phuwajaroanpong et al., In vitro and in vivo antiplasmodial activities and acute oral toxicity of Blumea balsamifera leaf extracts, Plants 2026 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13708541/

cards.front: Short note: Screening methods for hypolipidaemic activity

points: Serum total cholesterol, triglycerides, LDL-cholesterol and HDL-cholesterol.
The fractions move separately: in the Triton study every carboxamide derivative lowered triglycerides, but only one lowered total cholesterol.
Atherogenic ratios (TC/HDL, LDL/HDL, TG/HDL and the atherogenic index of plasma) summarise the effect on risk.
Triton WR-1339, a nonionic detergent, stops extrahepatic tissues from taking up circulating lipoproteins, so plasma lipids rise after a single dose (measured at 20 h in the rat study).
Groups: normal control, hyperlipidaemic control, a standard drug (fenofibrate in the rat study, atorvastatin 10 mg/kg in the mouse study) and each test compound at its chosen dose.
Blood is taken at 20-24 h and the lipid profile is measured on an automated analyser.
A single-dose model gives a fast answer on lipid lowering, not the effect of chronic treatment.
Rats fed a high-fat diet for about 4 weeks become hyperlipidaemic; in the cited study the powder or extract was then given daily for 28 days.
At the end the animals are anaesthetised, blood is taken by cardiac puncture for the same lipid profile, and body weight, food and water intake and organ weights are recorded.
Liver and kidney markers (AST, ALT, creatinine, urea) are measured in the same animals.
Each fraction is compared with the hyperlipidaemic control and, where one is used, with the standard drug; dose-dependence is looked for.
TC/HDL, LDL/HDL, TG/HDL and the atherogenic index of plasma are followed alongside the fractions.
A lipid fall is read together with liver and kidney markers and organ weights, so that it is not confused with toxicity.

WEB PMC Bekkouch et al., Hypolipidemic effects of Zingiber officinale and Citrus limon juices in a Triton model, PLoS One 2025 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12431240/

cards.front: How does Triton WR-1339 raise plasma lipids?
cards.back: It blocks the uptake of circulating lipoproteins by extrahepatic tissues, so triglyceride-, cholesterol- and LDL-rich particles accumulate in plasma after a single dose; this is the basis of the acute hyperlipidaemia screen.
refs: WEB PMC Alwahsh et al., Carboxamide derivatives in Triton WR-1339 induced hyperlipidemic rats, Lipids Health Dis 2025 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12164116/
